Spring Valley.wildlife_intro:
Spring Valley keeps our crew busy with raccoons and gray squirrels in attics, and striped skunks around yards and outbuildings. Hudson River, Harriman and Bear Mountain State Parks, Rockland Lake  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Spring Valley. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Spring Valley jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

The Pascack Brook runs right through the village before it crosses into New Jersey, and that wet corridor explains a lot of our Spring Valley work. Raccoons den in the older wood-frame homes along the brook and work the storm drains at night, skunks dig under the porches and shed slabs in the denser blocks off Main Street, and squirrels move through the mature street trees from roof to roof without ever touching the ground. Because so much of the village was built before modern sealing standards — and plenty of homes have had porches enclosed and additions tacked on over the decades — the gaps at rooflines and foundations here are bigger and more numerous than in the newer suburbs further up the county.

Spring Valley also sits in the path of everything moving between Harriman State Park's forest and the Hudson. Groundhogs burrow along the rail embankments and the back fences of the quieter streets up the hill, and bat colonies turn up in the attics of the tall older homes near the village center, where the louvered vents and chimney flashing have had a century to loosen. Our inspections here start at the chimney and work down: cap, flashing, soffit returns, then the basement rim and the garage corners, because in this housing stock the entry is rarely just one hole.
Spring Valley.extendedBody:
What Spring Valley's housing hands to wildlife

Spring Valley is one of the oldest, densest villages in Rockland County, and its houses show it. Flat and low-slope roofs downtown pond water and rot out their own fascia. Fieldstone and early concrete-block foundations have mortar joints that crumble into ready-made rat and skunk entries at grade. Enclosed porches — a signature Spring Valley conversion — create hollow voids underneath that skunks and groundhogs claim every spring, and the homeowner usually finds out from the smell through the floorboards, not from seeing the animal.

The animals we handle most in Spring Valley

Raccoons come first: they are a New York rabies-vector species, they den in chimneys and attic voids all over the village, and a female with kits in a flue needs a different job than a single winter squatter. Gray squirrels run the canopy streets and chew in at soffit returns, especially where limbs overhang the roof. Skunks work the Pascack Brook corridor and the grubs in the small lawns, and bats summer in the tall attics near the center of the village. Our work is done by a DEC-licensed Nuisance Wildlife Control Operator, and because New York does not allow animals to be moved off a property and released, everything here is exclusion, on-site release where the law allows it, and sealing — never a trap dumped in a park somewhere.

How a Spring Valley job runs

We inspect the whole structure, not just the hole you found: roofline, vents, chimney, foundation, and the porch and deck voids underneath. Then we get the animal out, seal every entry in metal and masonry-grade materials a raccoon cannot pull apart, and clean up droppings and nesting so the smell that advertises the den to the next animal is gone. If a raccoon or skunk has been handled, cornered, or is acting strangely, we will tell you plainly about rabies precautions and who to call — that conversation is part of the job in Rockland County.

faqs.q: There are bats in my Nyack Victorian every summer. When can they be excluded?
faqs.a: Bat work is exclusion only, and the timing matters: during the summer maternity season, flightless pups are in the colony, so a full exclusion then would trap them inside. We inspect and map every entry at any time of year, seal the secondary gaps, and schedule the one-way exclusion for when the young are flying — that scheduling is standard professional practice here, and it is the difference between solving the colony and making it worse. A bat found inside your living space is different: call us the same day.

faqs.q: A groundhog is undermining my retaining wall. Is that urgent?
faqs.a: More urgent than most groundhog calls, yes. On Nyack's slopes a burrow system can run several metres under a terraced wall, and every season of digging removes more of the soil the wall stands on. We remove the groundhog, then backfill and compact the burrow runs so the system does not collapse or get re-claimed. If the wall has already started to lean or crack, we will show you exactly where the burrows meet it so your mason sees the whole picture.

Nyack is built on a slope, and the slope runs the wildlife work here. Streets climb steeply from the Hudson waterfront up toward Hook Mountain, and every retaining wall, terraced garden, and hillside foundation on that climb is groundhog and skunk habitat. The big Victorian and colonial-revival homes along Broadway and the side streets give bats and squirrels a different kind of opening: tall attics, decorative soffits, and a hundred years of small gaps at every roof junction. Raccoons still work the storm drains along the waterfront and den in the older homes above the business district, and the wooded ravines that cut down through South Nyack carry deer, skunks, and the occasional coyote right through residential blocks. Our Nyack inspections pay special attention to hillside foundations and the backs of houses that face the ravines — those rear elevations are where entries hide, because nobody looks at them from the street.
Nyack.extendedBody:
Victorians, hillsides, and the Hudson: Nyack's three wildlife zones

Downtown Nyack's older homes are the bat and squirrel work: tall gabled roofs, ornate eaves, and chimney flashing that has been patched in layers since before anyone can remember. Bats slip in at gaps along the ridge and the chimney shoulders; gray squirrels chew in where branches from the big street trees reach the roof. On the slope above downtown, the job changes — groundhogs undermining terraced walls and garden beds, skunks denning under hillside decks, and raccoons in the attics of the view homes. Along the river itself, Norway rats work the shoreline rocks, the storm drains, and the older commercial buildings, and pigeons and starlings take over unused sign structures and loading areas.

Working on the river side of Rockland

Every Nyack job is done by a DEC-licensed Nuisance Wildlife Control Operator. Bats are exclusion only — we seal the secondary gaps, fit one-way valves at the active entries, and time full exclusions around the summer maternity season as professional practice, so flightless young are never sealed inside. Raccoons and skunks are New York rabies-vector species, so a animal behaving oddly in daylight gets treated with caution and reported the way the health department asks. And because New York does not permit moving an animal off the property, our answer to a den is always the same: get it out, then build the seal that makes the den useless.

What we check on a Nyack call

Roofline and chimney first, then the downhill foundation wall and any deck or porch void on the slope, then the attic itself for droppings, staining, and the rub marks that tell us how long the traffic has been running. Hillside homes often have a second, hidden problem — a groundhog burrow system under a retaining wall that is slowly taking the wall with it. We flag that when we find it, because fixing the burrow early is far cheaper than rebuilding the wall.

faqs.a: Black bears are permit-gated in New York: even a licensed Nuisance Wildlife Control Operator cannot remove one without a special DEC depredation permit, so bear problems go to the regional DEC wildlife office. What we can do is audit what is drawing it — feeders, garbage, pet food — and proof the structures other wildlife use. For raccoons, squirrels, and skunks, the Suffern regulars, our crew handles removal and sealing directly.

Suffern.wildlife_intro:
Suffern is Rockland's western gateway village, tucked against the Ramapo Mountains at the New Jersey line, where the Mahwah River runs through town and Harriman's forests begin a mile from the last residential street. That mountain edge drives its calls: raccoons and squirrels in the older village attics, black-bear country beyond the yards (bear problems themselves belong to DEC, not a booking), and skunks working the wooded lots. The village core is compact pre-war housing; the outskirts climb into rocky, wooded streets.

Rock and slope shape Suffern inspections — stone foundations, terraced lots, and roofs stepped up hillsides. Fall pushes squirrels and raccoons down from the mountain woods into the village housing; spring litters turn up in chimneys across the older streets. Our crew inspects Suffern homes completely, removes the animals, and seals entries stone to shingle, and we will tell you honestly when a complaint — a bear at the feeder, for instance — is a DEC call rather than ours.

faqs.a: The neighborhoods were built within a few years of each other, so their soffits, vents, and caps age out together — and the maturing street canopy now bridges straight onto the roofs. When one New City home gets squirrels in October, its neighbors are usually a season behind. Our crew seals the whole entry set so your house is not next on the same street's list.

New City.wildlife_intro:
New City is Rockland County's seat and its suburban center — postwar subdivisions, the county offices, and shopping corridors, all under a maturing canopy with the Hackensack River's headwaters and Lake DeForest's watershed lands nearby. Its wildlife work is high-volume suburb work: gray squirrels in the soffits of 1960s and 1970s homes, raccoons in their chimneys, and groundhogs and skunks on the larger lots toward the town's rural northern end.

Subdivisions built in one era fail in patterns, and New City is old enough that its first-generation soffits, vents, and chimney caps are failing together across whole neighborhoods. Our crew inspects New City homes against that pattern — every vent type, not just the active one — removes the animals, and seals the full set. Spring raccoon litters and the fall squirrel rush are both heavy here, and early calls in either season stay small jobs.

faqs.q: Why are rats a recurring problem in Haverstraw?
faqs.a: Brick-era worker housing on older foundations, a working riverfront, and tight commercial blocks give Norway rats harborage, food, and travel routes within a few yards of most village homes. The lasting fix is removal plus below-grade sealing — foundation gaps, drain openings, and utility penetrations — which our crew maps at inspection rather than guessing from the attic down.

Haverstraw.wildlife_intro:
Haverstraw is the Hudson's old brickmaking capital, a dense riverfront village where brick worker housing climbs from the shore toward High Tor's ridge. Density defines its wildlife work: Norway rats in the oldest blocks and around the riverfront, raccoons and squirrels in the tightly packed attics, and pigeons and starlings on the downtown commercial roofs. The wooded ridge behind the village supplies a steady flow of animals into the streets below it.

In a village this dense, wildlife is a block-level condition: shared rooflines, connected yards, and alleyways mean one property's opening serves several buildings. Our crew inspects Haverstraw homes with the neighbors' junctions in view, removes the animals, and seals the entries — and for rat work we start below grade, at the foundations and drains of the brick housing, where this village's rat problems actually live.

Our crew identifies the tenant, removes it, and screens the shed and deck perimeters so the space stays vacant.

Clarkstown towns.wildlife_intro:
This page covers the rest of Clarkstown beyond New City — the hamlets of Congers, Valley Cottage, Bardonia, and West Nyack, where Rockland's suburban fabric loosens into lake neighborhoods, reservoir watershed, and larger wooded lots. Congers sits between two lakes, DeForest and Swartwout, and its homes get lake-edge raccoons and skunks; Valley Cottage adds the Rockland Lake State Park edge; Bardonia and West Nyack are classic postwar suburbia with squirrel-heavy canopy streets.

Two lakes and a state park inside one town means ground-level wildlife is as busy as the rooflines: groundhogs under sheds on the big lots, skunks under porches near the water, opossums everywhere. Our crew inspects Clarkstown hamlet homes whole — attic, foundation, and yard structures — removes the animals, and seals or screens what the inspection found, so a Congers lake house and a Bardonia ranch each get the version of the job their lot actually needs.
